abilities.name: Decree of the Dead
abilities.description: Declares what is owed to the dead and their realm, told aloud to everyone present and recorded as a legend.

relationships.note: They are two of three brothers who drew lots for their realms, and Zeus gave him Persephone. The starting value is authored tuning.

lore.statement: Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades are brothers. They drew lots: Hades got the murky underworld, Poseidon the grey sea, Zeus the broad sky.
The halls of Hades and Persephone stand with a dog at the gate that fawns on those who enter and will not let them leave.
Hades carries Persephone off in his chariot, given to him by Zeus.
Zeus sends Hermes to bid Hades release Persephone. Hades gives her a pomegranate seed to eat, and she spends a third of each year below and the rest among the gods.
Hades is not to be soothed or overcome, and so is the most hated by mortals of all the gods.
The dead are judged by Minos, who sits with a golden sceptre in Hades' wide-gated house with the dead around him; the sources do not make Hades the judge.

variants.note: In the Iliad Hades is the one who will not be soothed. In the Hymn to Demeter he yields to Zeus's command and gives Persephone a seed that binds her to return. The profile keeps both: he holds what is his, and keeps a bargain he has made.

inventions.statement: Hades's domain troubles are the game's own.
inventions.reason: A buried hoard swallowed, a dig that collapses, and a buried ore seam lost are troubles the game draws on a season's odds and a floor, taking goods. None needs a death. Two things are attested: Iliad 15.187-193 gives him the murky underworld as his lot, and Plato's Cratylus 403a says only that the name Pluto is from wealth that comes up from below out of the earth. Neither tells a hoard swallowed, a dig that collapses, or an ore seam lost: the Iliad lines cited for the hoard and the dig are the lot's, and the Cratylus line cited for the seam is the wealth's, not the seam's.

inventions.statement: His decrees on the dead's due are told in play as legends.
inventions.reason: Legend is the world's only public telling; it is a game mapping.

inventions.statement: Judging the dead and claiming them are not abilities here.
inventions.reason: The sources give the judging to Minos, and the world has no death rule yet (M3). The game gives Hades only a decree.

inventions.statement: No new mortals live in the underworld.
inventions.reason: No mortal lives in the underworld, and the dead are an M3 matter. Hades's stake in the living town is one devotee above ground: the ferryman (see ferryman-rites).

inventions.statement: The ferryman at the town's Styx ferry dock reveres Hades, so prayers to him come from the one place the living town meets the road of the dead.
inventions.reason: Hades's sources here give him the dead, the underworld, and the Persephone bargain, and name no ferryman; Hermes leading souls down (Odyssey 24.1-14) is in Hermes's profile, not this one. The ferry, its keeper, and the devotion are the game's, so that Hades has a prayer to answer and, with Hermes, something to contend over.

inventions.statement: The drive weights and the starting dispositions of Hades are authored tuning.
inventions.reason: The sources describe temperament in prose; the numbers are a design choice to be revised against play.

troubles.statement: A buried hoard is swallowed by the earth: coin is lost. Autumn and winter.
A dig collapses and buries ore. Spring and autumn.
A buried ore seam is lost: ore or tools are lost. Winter.
